title: Breathing
subtitle: About twelve times a minute, all day, without a thought
intro: Point at any part to see what it does. Watch the chest breathe, or start the tour to follow one breath from the throat to the lungs and back.

structures.name: Epiglottis
structures.summary: A leaf-shaped flap at the back of the tongue. It folds down over the windpipe when you swallow, so food goes to the stomach and not the lungs.
structures.fact: When something goes down the wrong way, the flap has missed, and a cough pushes it back out.

structures.name: Thyroid cartilage
structures.summary: The largest cartilage of the voice box. It shields the vocal cords, and in many men it forms the bump called the Adam's apple.
structures.fact: Its name comes from the Greek for shield.

structures.name: Vocal process
structures.summary: A small projection of cartilage in the voice box. The vocal cords attach to it, and moving it tightens or slackens them to change your pitch.
structures.fact: Your voice is air from the lungs making the cords vibrate.

structures.name: Windpipe and bronchi
structures.summary: The windpipe, about 12 cm long, and the tubes that branch from it into each lung. Rings of cartilage hold it open.
structures.fact: The branches divide about 23 times, ending in some 480 million tiny air sacs.

structures.name: Right lung
structures.summary: It has three lobes and is a little bigger than the left. Air reaches the tiny sacs at its ends, where oxygen passes into the blood.
structures.fact: Lungs have no muscle of their own. The chest and the diaphragm pull them open.

structures.name: Left lung
structures.summary: It has two lobes, and a notch in its edge makes room for the heart.
structures.fact: Together the lungs hold about six litres when full, yet a normal breath moves only about half a litre.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.summary: The main muscle of breathing, a dome under the lungs. It tightens and flattens to pull air in, and relaxes to let it out.
structures.fact: A hiccup is the diaphragm twitching suddenly.

structures.name: Ribs
structures.summary: Twelve pairs of curved bones that protect the heart and lungs. They swing up and out as you breathe in.
structures.fact: The lowest two pairs are called floating ribs because they do not reach the front.

structures.name: Costal cartilage
structures.summary: Flexible cartilage that joins most of the ribs to the breastbone, letting the chest spring open and back.
structures.fact: It slowly turns to bone with age, which makes the chest a little stiffer.

structures.name: Breastbone
structures.summary: The flat bone at the front of the chest. It moves up and forward a little with each breath.
structures.fact: In CPR the chest is pressed here, to squeeze the heart against the spine.

structures.name: Hyoid bone
structures.summary: A small U-shaped bone under the tongue that holds the tongue and the voice box in place.
structures.fact: It is the only bone in the body that does not join another bone.

structures.name: Cricoid cartilage
structures.summary: The ring of cartilage at the top of the windpipe, just below the thyroid cartilage.
structures.fact: It is the only complete ring in the airway.

structures.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
structures.summary: A sheet of tissue joining the hyoid bone to the thyroid cartilage.
structures.fact: Nerves and blood vessels pass through it to the voice box.

structures.name: Cricothyroid ligament
structures.summary: A tough band linking the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
structures.fact: Doctors can make an emergency airway through it.

tour.caption: Air comes in through the nose or mouth and passes the epiglottis, the flap that keeps food out of the airway.
It flows through the voice box, where air passing the vocal cords makes your voice.
Down the windpipe it goes, which divides into two branches, one for each lung.
The branches divide again and again, ending in about 480 million tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood.
To draw a breath in, the diaphragm tightens and flattens, pulling the lungs down.
At the same time the ribs swing up and out and the breastbone lifts, widening the chest.
The lungs stretch to fill the space, and air rushes in. Then the muscles relax, the chest springs back, and the air flows out.
